clue.text: A strong hand in clubs

blocks.note: surface reading: a powerful card holding in the suit of clubs at bridge
setter's reading: a hand is a worker, and a strong one employed at nightclubs keeps order at the door

explanation.surface: A bridge player holds a powerful set of cards in the club suit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand' and 'clubs' both pull towards card games; read hand as a hired worker and clubs as nightclubs.
explanation.definitionFit: A bouncer is the burly doorman employed by a nightclub to keep out or eject troublemakers.

clue.text: Pick up the bill, a case for hard foreign currency

indicators.note: in a down clue, picking something up lifts it, so its letters read from the bottom upward
a case holds something inside it, so the first word wraps around the second

blocks.note: a tab is a bill, as in picking up the tab at a bar
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Someone offers to settle the restaurant bill in a hard foreign currency.
explanation.walkthrough: TAB reversed gives BAT, which then holds H.
explanation.definitionFit: The baht is the monetary unit of Thailand, so it is a currency from abroad.

clue.text: State university raising capital investment

indicators.note: raising lifts something up, and in a down entry that means the letters read upward

blocks.note: U is the standard abbreviation for university
an investment can be clothing one is invested with, and a hat is worn on the head, or capital

explanation.surface: A state university is putting more money into its capital projects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital investment' sounds financial, but capital is the head and an investment is something put on, so it means a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Utah is one of the fifty states of the USA.

clue.text: Invitation that is about work inspires poets

definitions.note: a verb phrase describing the noun answer, the muse who does this

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the abbreviation for that is goes round the word for work

blocks.note: a call is a summons or invitation
i.e. is the Latin abbreviation for that is
OP, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: A call to join a writing project gives poets their inspiration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspires poets' looks like a verb, but it describes the muse who does the inspiring; the abbreviation for that is is split to hold the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Calliope is the Greek muse of epic poetry, the goddess who inspires poets.

clue.text: Right! Breathe out and relax!

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
to breathe out is to emit or send forth air

explanation.surface: A yoga instructor tells the class: right, now exhale and unwind.
explanation.definitionFit: To remit can mean to slacken or ease off, as a fever or effort is lessened.

clue.text: Sort of pastry brought round to spoil the appetite

indicators.note: something brought round another thing encircles it, so one word goes around the other

blocks.note: puff is a light flaky kind of pastry
taken as written

explanation.surface: A soggy pastry served at the table ruins diners' hunger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' looks like part of the definition, but it is the word that PUFF wraps.
explanation.definitionFit: To be put off food is to lose one's desire to eat, so put off can mean deter or dull the appetite.

clue.text: Ignorant and under a misconception

indicators.note: a misconception is a mistaken idea, suggesting the letters have been wrongly put together

blocks.note: taken as written, the article included

explanation.surface: Someone uninformed is labouring under a false belief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under a misconception' reads as one idiom, but the first two words are the fodder and the last signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Unread describes a person who has not read widely and is therefore poorly educated.

clue.text: Put on too much weight

blocks.note: surface reading: became overweight by eating too much
setter's reading: had too heavy a burden placed on it, like a lorry or circuit

explanation.surface: Someone has gained more pounds than is healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something overloaded has been given a burden heavier than it was built to bear.

clue.text: Plenty of suckers at this trading centre?

blocks.clueFragment: Plenty of suckers at this trading centre?
blocks.note: surface reading: a place full of gullible buyers ready to be fleeced
setter's reading: bloodsucking insects, as if the market were stocked with them

explanation.surface: A cynic remarks that a market is crawling with easily duped customers.
explanation.walkthrough: A sucker is a dupe and also a bloodsucking parasite; the name of this second-hand market suggests the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A flea market is an outdoor street market selling cheap second-hand goods.

clue.text: Light equipment for miner and motorist

definitions.text: Light equipment for miner and motorist

blocks.note: surface reading: lightweight gear carried by workers
setter's reading: a lamp, worn on a miner's helmet or fitted to the front of a car

explanation.surface: A shop sells portable kit suited to both mineworkers and drivers.
explanation.definitionFit: A headlamp is a lamp on a miner's helmet and also a headlight at the front of a car.

clue.text: Fat, it is said, of the land

indicators.note: it is said tells us to go by how a word is spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: grease is animal fat

explanation.surface: It sounds like a phrase about the fat of the land, meaning rich living.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'fat of the land' means abundance, hiding where the definition starts.
explanation.definitionFit: Greece is a Mediterranean country, so it is a land or nation.

clue.text: One in favour of half-day closing

blocks.note: the first half of Friday, the usual abbreviation for that day
a closing is an end

explanation.surface: Someone supports shops shutting for an afternoon each week.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-day closing was a British custom of shops closing one afternoon a week. FRI is half of Friday.
explanation.definitionFit: A friend of a cause is a supporter or backer of it.

clue.text: Suitable fruit for queen of puddings?

definitions.text: Suitable fruit for queen of puddings

blocks.note: surface reading: the traditional British dessert of custard, jam and meringue
setter's reading: a fruit named after a monarch would suit a queen's pudding

explanation.surface: A cook asks which fruit goes best in a queen of puddings.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen of puddings is a British baked dessert; the queen here is the one the fruit is named after.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victoria plum is a popular English variety of red plum, named after the queen.

clue.text: Practice of making personal deliveries

blocks.note: surface reading: a courier handing parcels over in person
setter's reading: the births of babies, which a medical specialist attends

explanation.surface: A courier firm boasts of handing every parcel over in person.
explanation.definitionFit: Obstetrics is the branch of medicine concerned with childbirth, so its practitioners deliver babies.

clue.text: Flying saucer?

blocks.note: surface reading: an alien spacecraft or UFO
setter's reading: a saucer-shaped disc of baked earth flung into the air as a target

explanation.walkthrough: The disc used in trap shooting is shaped like a small saucer and is launched to fly through the air.
explanation.definitionFit: A clay pigeon is a disc thrown up as a target for shotgun shooting.

clue.text: One who sticks at his job and mails his account?

definitions.text: One who sticks at his job

blocks.clueFragment: One who sticks at his job and mails his account?
blocks.note: surface reading: a diligent worker who sends off his invoice
setter's reading: one who pastes up notices, and also one who posts a bill

explanation.surface: A conscientious tradesman keeps at the work, then sends out his invoice.
explanation.walkthrough: Sticking and posting are both literal: a bill is a poster, and posting a bill is also mailing an account.
explanation.definitionFit: A billposter is someone employed to paste advertising posters onto walls and hoardings.

clue.text: They include a case for those seeking a rise

definitions.text: They include a case for those seeking a rise

blocks.clueFragment: include a case for those seeking a rise
blocks.note: surface reading: workers presenting arguments for a pay increase
setter's reading: add the word case and you have the structure people climb to go up

explanation.surface: Employees putting forward a strong argument for higher pay.
explanation.walkthrough: A staircase is these plus case, and people use them to go up.
explanation.definitionFit: Steps leading from one floor to another are what people climb to reach a higher level.

clue.text: Inspired piece of music

definitions.note: past participle; the answer is the thing breathed in

blocks.note: first meaning: what is drawn into the lungs when breathing in
second meaning: a tune or melody

explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspired' looks like praise for the music, but read literally it means breathed in.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the gas mixture we breathe and a simple melodic tune or song.

clue.text: Guard of honour

blocks.note: surface reading: a ceremonial line of soldiers
setter's reading: a young woman's reputation, protected by an older companion

explanation.walkthrough: A guard of honour is ceremonial troops, but here it is someone guarding a young woman's good name.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaperon accompanies a young unmarried woman in public to protect her reputation and propriety.

clue.text: Essay that won't be pointless

blocks.note: first meaning: an attempt
second meaning: a rugby touchdown, which always scores points

explanation.surface: A student hopes an essay will have a point to it.
explanation.walkthrough: Essay as a verb or noun means an attempt; in rugby a try earns five points.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means an effort or attempt, and also a scoring touchdown in rugby football.

clue.text: He crashed awkwardly before the end of the race - bad luck!

indicators.note: doing something awkwardly means clumsily, so the letters come out in a jumbled order
the end of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of race

explanation.surface: A racing driver crashed just before the finish line, what a shame!
explanation.walkthrough: Hard cheese is a British expression of mock sympathy, meaning tough luck.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard cheese is a British idiom used to commiserate, often unsympathetically, over misfortune.

clue.text: Is of one mind about grease

indicators.note: about can mean around or in a different position, so the letters are moved round

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Everyone holds the same opinion on lubrication.
explanation.definitionFit: To agree is to share an opinion, so someone who agrees is in accord with another.

clue.text: Too eager to press for expulsion from chambers

blocks.clueFragment: Too eager to press for expulsion from chambers
blocks.note: surface reading: overzealous in pushing for someone to be thrown out of a parliament or barristers' offices
setter's reading: the chambers of a gun, from which a press of the finger expels bullets

explanation.surface: An overzealous politician pushes hard for a member to be thrown out of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: Chambers suggests a legislature or barristers' offices; here they are the chambers of a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone trigger-happy is too quick to fire a gun, or more widely to act rashly.

clue.text: A huge shipping order?

blocks.note: taken as written
vast means huge

explanation.surface: A company places an enormous order for freight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shipping order' suggests a commercial consignment; here it is a command given on board ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Avast is a sailor's command meaning stop or cease, an order heard at sea.

clue.text: Found to be contemptible

blocks.note: first meaning: to establish or ground something
second meaning: low, mean and despicable

explanation.surface: Someone has been judged worthy of scorn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' reads as the past of find, but it is the verb meaning establish.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works as a verb for grounding or establishing and as an adjective for morally low.

clue.text: Punch about the body

blocks.note: first meaning: to hit hard
second meaning: a strap worn around the waist

explanation.surface: A boxer lands a blow to the torso.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About the body' sounds like where a punch lands; it is a second definition for a strap that goes round the waist.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is slang for a hard blow and also names a strap worn around the waist.

clue.text: Wild kids grow up to be adults like these

blocks.note: surface reading: unruly children reaching adulthood
setter's reading: young goats living in the wild, which mature into mountain goats

explanation.surface: Unruly youngsters eventually mature into grown-ups.
explanation.walkthrough: Kids are young goats, and the wild ones become these mountain goats.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibexes are wild mountain goats with long curved horns, and their young are called kids.

clue.text: It warrants attack, but there must be no cheating in it

definitions.text: there must be no cheating in it

blocks.note: first meaning: a legitimate target for criticism or pursuit

blocks.clueFragment: there must be no cheating in it
blocks.note: second meaning: a contest played honestly

explanation.surface: A target deserves to be attacked, but the contest must be clean.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means a legitimate target, while read literally it is a sporting contest played honestly.

clue.text: The most logical form of assent

indicators.note: a form of something is a version of it in another shape, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Agreement is the most reasonable response.
explanation.definitionFit: Sanest is the superlative of sane, meaning most rational and sensible in thinking.

clue.text: Get browned off with a chap on the Circle Line?

blocks.note: to tan is to become browned by the sun
a gent, short for gentleman, is a chap

explanation.surface: A sunburnt man rides the Circle Line on the London Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: The Circle Line is a London Underground route; read it as a line touching a circle, and 'off' recalls going off at a tangent.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a tangent is a straight line touching a circle at exactly one point.
